rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because makr can be positive, qualifying it as evil identifies the schemes as malicious; verse 10 also alludes to their conspiracies and fate.
rows.anchor: qualifies it to refer to the nature of these schemes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A plot against truth turns first against its maker: opposing a truth-guide leads the plotter astray and ruins his own fate, while he cannot harm others without God's permission.
rows.anchor: anyone who conspires against the truth in fact conspires against his own self

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here yanzurūn means waiting, and ellipsis supplies God's practice toward earlier peoples: the deniers are awaiting the same destruction that befell nations who denied their messengers.
rows.anchor: In other words, if because of their arrogance and aversion from the truth, these people have taken to opposing it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's established practice neither changes between nations nor fails to occur at its appointed time; this assures the Prophet that no one can stop it.
rows.anchor: the practice of God neither changes nor fails to materialize

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ruins of divinely punished nations in Arabia show that earlier, mightier peoples met this fate for denying God's prophets; Quraysh have passed these ruins without learning, though they still can reflect.
rows.anchor: have in fact moved about in the land a lot and have passed by the ruins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh cannot match those nations in strength, and none escapes God's comprehensive knowledge and power; He sees all and has power over everything.
rows.anchor: There is nothing in the heavens and earth which is beyond His grasp

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will punish wrongdoers, but defers punishment to an appointed term to allow repentance and remove excuses; once the term ends, He determines their fate.
rows.anchor: He gives respite to people till an appointed time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An ellipsis after “what they earned” is understood from the following contrast that God defers their punishment.
rows.anchor: What is suppressed is evident from the words

none: Date and closing publication mark only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recalls a town warned by two messengers, then a third helper; its people rejected them, blamed the warning signs, threatened them, and were destroyed.
rows.anchor: two messengers were sent by God to warn its people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cosmic signs in this passage call for gratitude whose necessary expression is monotheism, and they also entail a day of reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: all these signs entail gratitude to God and the essential requirement of this gratitude is monotheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who demand punishment and resist spending for God's cause should know that its arrival needs no preparation and will seize everyone suddenly.
rows.anchor: it will come in the blink of an eye and catch everyone unaware

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah depicts resurrection, the contrasting fates of believers and rejecters, and the testimony of people's limbs on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The events of the Day of Judgement are portrayed and the fates of the believers and rejecters are depicted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment-demanders are warned to use their faculties and reason: God can remove sight or deform them, though their respite reflects His mercy.
rows.anchor: they should benefit from the abilities of sight and hearing which the Almighty has blessed them with

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section resumes the opening themes of monotheism and the Hereafter and assures the Prophet that he awakens the morally living, not the dead-hearted.
rows.anchor: what was discussed in the opening one is take up again in a different style

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yā Sīn consists of disconnected letters and is the sūrah's Qur'anic name.
rows.anchor: These letters are from among the muqat@t@a‘āt h@urūf

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some interpret Yā Sīn as “O human,” but the author rejects this interpretation as unsupported.
rows.anchor: Some people think that it means

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Farāhī, the author takes the waw as an oath that functions as testimony: the wise Qur'an bears witness that Muhammad is among the messengers.
rows.anchor: in Arabic an oath itself signifies bearing witness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger's wise miraculous discourse establishes that the Qur'an bears witness to his prophethood; its real miracle is wisdom and philosophy, with eloquence additional.
rows.anchor: miraculous discourse. It is thus evident that the real miracle of the Qur’ān lies in its wisdom and philosophy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second predicate without a conjunction shows the Qur'an testifies both to Muhammad's prophethood and his straight path and call; the indefinite phrase magnifies the path, which accords with divine guidance, intellect, and nature.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān simultaneously bears witness to two things

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tanzīl is accusative after an omitted verb and can mean gradual, thorough revelation; the Mighty warns deniers while the Merciful reveals the Book as mercy and guidance for those who value it.
rows.anchor: it also means to reveal something gradually in a thorough and profound manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation commissions Muhammad to warn the Ishmaelites, whose forebears had no prophet, ending their heedlessness; this fulfills Abraham's prayer and prophetic predictions, while warning that neglecting the favor brings devastation.
rows.anchor: Reference here is to the Ishmaelites and the verse actually states the great favour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage parallels the statement that a people had received no warner before the Prophet.
rows.anchor: so that you inform people to whom no warner had come before you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “word” is God's response to Satan's threat: He would fill Hell with humans and jinn who follow him; the Prophet must warn without expecting everyone to believe or worrying over rejecters destined for Hell.
rows.anchor: the statement of God given by Him in response to Satan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yokes reaching the chins portray arrogant rejecters unable to lower their heads or see the signs in earth and heaven; God ascribes this condition to Himself as punishment under His established law.
rows.anchor: it is as if yolks have been put around their necks which rise up till the chins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muqmaḥ describes a camel tied from behind so its head cannot bend; the fixed neck angle depicts arrogance and leaves such people unaware of surrounding signs, absorbed only in ego.
rows.anchor: Exactly same will be the case of a person around whose neck an iron yolk will be put

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who knowingly evade truth and ignore God's signs are punished when their desires and evil deeds dominate them, so reminders no longer affect them; this is the heart-rust law described in al-Muṭaffifīn.
rows.anchor: the rust of their deeds has settled on their hearts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barriers and veiled eyes explain the rejecters' blindness; Sabaʾ asks why they did not see heaven and earth before and behind them, while past traditions and future ambitions obstruct their sight.
rows.anchor: such arrogant people are slave to their past traditions and future ambitions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warnings cannot make these intellectually and morally diseased people believe, though they establish the proof so they cannot plead ignorance; see the discussion of sealing hearts at al-Baqarah's opening.
rows.anchor: to warn them or to not warn them is absolutely useless

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reminders benefit those who heed counsel, open their hearts, and reason beyond the senses; valuable faith is professed through sight, hearing, mind, and heart before direct visual proof, while the Prophet leaves sight-demanders to God.
rows.anchor: Only that faith is of value to God which is professed by using the faculties of sight, hearing, mind as well as the heart

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of God follows from His graciousness: He must reward the pious and punish wrongdoers, so the appointed Day displays mercy and justice perfectly.
rows.anchor: For the manifestation of His graciousness, He has appointed a day for reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will resurrect the dead and record their deeds and traces; this entails judgment according to deeds, an implication left unstated because it is evident, while deniers doubt resurrection and another aspect of judgment.
rows.anchor: this necessarily means that He will deal with each of them according to his or her deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs no preparation to punish the Quraysh; His mercy alone explains the respite, and one blast will seize people before they can make a will or return home.
rows.anchor: a single blast from God will be such that everyone will be seized by it wherever they are

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Section IV compares the instantaneous worldly blast with resurrection at the trumpet, portrays judgment and the separate fates, then warns that God can swiftly remove people's abilities; delay is mercy.
rows.anchor: At the sound of the trumpet everyone will be raised to life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As with the threatened worldly punishment in 36:48–49, the Hereafter requires no preparation: the trumpet immediately sends people running to their Lord; challengers should use the respite to repent.
rows.anchor: Now, in this verse it is said that the matter of the Hereafter is no different

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grave-raisers' question expresses shock and misfortune rather than seeking information: the event they called a bluff has come true.
rows.anchor: This question will not be meant to elicit an answer

rows.speaker: the disbelievers
rows.claim: One possible reading has the resurrected deniers themselves admit that the Merciful's promise and the messengers' word have come true.
rows.anchor: they are uttered by these very people

rows.speaker: the angels
rows.claim: The author prefers that angels speak God's words to humiliate the deniers; al-Ṣāffāt parallels this and shows the final rebuke comes from God at the right time.
rows.anchor: I would prefer the second of these options because it is supported by parallel verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A single shout instantly assembles everyone before God; the claim continues on the next page.
rows.anchor: All this will happen in the blink of any eye merely by a shout from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs only one shout, not military preparations; jamiʿ emphasizes that nobles and commoners, rulers and ruled, worshippers and deities are all brought to Him like criminals in court.
rows.anchor: they shall be brought before the presence of God the way criminals are brought in a court

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present-tense style makes Judgment Day seem to be occurring now; its perfect justice lets no soul be wronged, since people reap only what they earned.
rows.anchor: the Day of Judgement has arrived and the addressees are being told about its arrival

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The undefined shughul magnifies Paradise's leisurely pursuits.
rows.anchor: occurs as an undefined noun to magnify its import

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning spouses shows that family completes the enjoyment; reclining on couches evokes the best royal sitting places and the eternal kingdom of Paradise.
rows.anchor: no leisurely pursuit is complete without one’s family

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise offers fruits and anything requested; the passage continues to explain the extent of that privilege.
rows.anchor: in Paradise they will be presented with fruits and moreover whatever else they ask for

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whatever its inhabitants demand means whatever they desire; unlike the greatest earthly kings, they can obtain it immediately.
rows.anchor: the greatest of kings in this world never had this status and position

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's salām is Paradise's greatest success; an omitted subject keeps focus on the predicate, with al-Aḥzāb 33:44 as a parallel, and reports say angels convey it or enter through every gate.
rows.anchor: is suppressed here so that all the attention of the addressee is focused on the enunciative

rows.speaker: unnamed poet
rows.claim: An Urdu couplet celebrates the glad tidings, presenting even the sacrifice of one's life for them as worthwhile.
rows.anchor: Even sacrificing one’s life on these glad tidings is acceptable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Judgment the wrongdoers must separate from believers: the former world was a shared place of trial, but now reward and punishment divide their worlds.
rows.anchor: now is the time of reward and punishment; hence they must now separate from the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAhida with ilā conveys obligation and guarantee; Adam's descendants were bound not to worship Satan, their enemy, but to worship God on the straight path.
rows.anchor: it encompasses the meaning of being made responsible of something and standing as guarantor to something

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's enmity and misleading of many show the people's failure to distinguish foe from friend; he deceived Adam's ancestors and his hostility continues to Judgment, as discussed in al-Baqarah and al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: it was Satan who deceived their forefathers and had them expelled from Paradise

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell is the promised fate the deniers were warned about by God's messengers and pious people; their denial leaves it as their abode.
rows.anchor: God’s messengers and His pious people warned them of this fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address shifts from direct rebuke to indirect portrayal of helplessness; sealed mouths cannot lie or excuse themselves, while hands and feet testify conclusively to deeds, as in al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: the tongue can lie and also present lame excuses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who fail to use God's gifts deserve their loss: He could erase their eyes and leave them unable to find the path; their continued sight is mercy and respite. The author also supplies an omitted conditional verb after law.
rows.anchor: If He wanted, He could have obliterated their eyes and then they would have been left to wonder about

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammatically, law is a past conditional particle; the author reconstructs an omitted kāna before the following verb.
rows.anchor: there is an incomplete verb suppressed before the indefinite verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God could deform people where they stand and prevent all movement, but graciously gives them time to mend their ways, recognize His favors, and be grateful.
rows.anchor: out of His grace God did not do this and had given respite to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human aging is an observable proof that God can reverse and distort human capacities: a newborn is weak, adolescence brings peak strength, and old age returns a person toward helplessness; the Qur'an also describes this arc.
rows.anchor: After that, old age afflicts a person and he gradually returns to a state of weakness and helplessness
